catalog_quote: So, is Urarina a stress, tonal or pitch accent language? We do not have an answer to that question yet. What makes it difficult to classify Urarina is that it presents properties that are stress-like and tonal-like while at the same time the assignment of its high pitch keeps making reference to syntactic information. ... In Urarina, each morpheme surfaces with only one high pitch. In the case of nouns, the high pitch has a window that constrains its location. This window corresponds to the last two syllables of the word. Thus, the high pitch of nouns can occur either on the penultimate or final syllable. The fact that high pitch seems to be bound to a syllable-based window on one of the word edges remind us of stress systems. new_statements.quote: So, is Urarina a stress, tonal or pitch accent language? We do not have an answer to that question yet. [...] In Urarina, each morpheme surfaces with only one high pitch. In the case of nouns, the high pitch has a window that constrains its location. This window corresponds to the last two syllables of the word. [...] As the subject of a sentence or in citation form, most nouns show a high pitch on the final syllable and only a few have it on the penultimate one. However, if those same nouns occur as the object of a verb, the nouns that had a high pitch on the final syllable when they were subjects, now have it on the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prominence is a single high pitch (f0 peak) per morpheme/word, marked with an acute. In nouns it is restricted to a final two-syllable window: in citation form and as subject the default (most nouns, 'Subject-pattern A') is H on the FINAL syllable; a lexically marked minority ('pattern B') has H on the PENULT. When the noun is the object of a verb the classes swap (A -> penult, B -> final). Object nouns additionally belong to four lexical classes that dictate where H falls on the following verb (initial, second, final syllable, or no H at all). H placement ignores vowel length (p. 159). The authors find no evidence of tonal contrast but explicitly refuse to classify the system as stress, tone or pitch accent; Olawsky 2006 analyses the same facts in a chapter titled 'Tone'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; each morpheme surfaces with only one high pitch, and a verb may surface with no high pitch at all depending on the class of its object noun.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically marked 'Subject-pattern B' nouns (penult H in citation form, e.g. [sabéde] 'machete', [enamána] 'young man'); a small set such as 'fox' [adʉlédi] with penult H in citation form but final H as object; loan 'machete' among pattern B; high pitch on verbs is entirely governed by the object noun's lexical class.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms and subject position pattern together (final H default); object position shifts H one syllable leftward and the object noun controls H on the adjacent verb, so the prominence is word-delimited (final two-syllable window) but syntactically conditioned. Declaratives end in L% boundary tone. Data: 5 male speakers, Nueva Esperanza (Upper Chambira), Praat f0 analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes Upper-Chambira Urarina (community of Nueva Esperanza, upper Río Chambira, Loreto), 10 male speakers recorded 2015/2018; Glottolog urar1246 has no dialect nodes, and Olawsky 2006 (ch. 23 'Variation') is the place to check for dialect differences in prosody. Language-level match: urar1246 / ISO ura.
